entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Francesco degli Atti (died September 2, 1361) was an influential Italian cardinal whose career spanned a critical period of the Avignon Papacy, demonstrating the complex interplay of ecclesiastical power, political maneuvering, and administrative reform within the fourteenth-century Church. Elevated to cardinal by Pope Innocent VI, his actions and counsel were integral to maintaining papal authority and managing the Church's vast financial and political apparatus during a time marked by widespread instability, including the aftermath of the Black Death and burgeoning conflicts in Italy.

Born into a prominent family, degli Atti began his ecclesiastical career in Italy before being appointed Bishop of Corneto (modern Tarquinia) and Montefiascone in 1353, positions that placed him at the nexus of papal temporal and spiritual influence. His elevation to cardinal-priest of San Marco in 1356 by Innocent VI solidified his role within the papal curia in Avignon. During his cardinalate, he was deeply involved in the intricate diplomatic efforts to restore order in the Papal States and to finance the Church's operations, often navigating competing interests of European monarchs and Italian city-states.

His contributions helped to stabilize the administrative machinery of the Avignon Papacy, providing continuity and expertise that were vital for the long-term governance of the Church. While he did not live to see the end of the Avignon period or the subsequent Great Western Schism, his work in strengthening papal finances and governance laid groundwork for later efforts to centralize papal power. His career exemplifies the critical role of skilled administrators in sustaining large, complex institutions through periods of profound change.
